items.title: Love at a Standstill — Italian Cold Wave Quartet Winter Severity Index Returns With Video for “Motionless”
items.summary: I knew you’re there Watching all my movements in the dark. I tried to call your name, But never reached the twinkling in your eyes. Love can make a spectacular… The post Love at a Standstill — Italian Cold Wave Quartet Winter Severity Index Returns With Video
items.fullText:
I knew you’re there
Watching all my movements in the dark.
I tried to call your name,
But never reached the twinkling in your eyes.

Love can make a spectacular fool of anybody with a functioning nervous system. You spend months, sometimes years, investing somebody with qualities they demonstrated on perhaps three occasions, sustaining yourself on the emotional equivalent of a handful of loose change. By the time you realize the relationship has become a private enterprise, with yourself as its sole employee, you’ve practically forgotten what life was like before you started working there. Simona Ferrucci sings from somewhere within this dreadful predicament on Motionless, the first single from Winter Severity Index’s fifteenth-anniversary album, The Brightest Days.

The Italian outfit marks the occasion by reuniting its original lineup: Ferrucci on vocals and guitar, Diana Salzo on bass, Valeria Tirabassi on drums, and Valentina Fanigliulo on synthesizers. Together, the four musicians revisit nine compositions from their formative years, reconsidering arrangements with the benefit of fifteen years spent developing their respective musical sensibilities.

Motionless makes a formidable argument for getting the old gang together. Salzo’s bass possesses that wonderfully oppressive physical presence familiar to anyone who has spent considerable portions of their adolescence listening to Faith and Pornography. Tirabassi establishes a relentless rhythmic foundation beneath guitars that dissolve into great, overlapping sheets of distortion, while Fanigliulo’s synthesizers introduce an almost celestial dimension to the proceedings. Somewhere between the desolate grandeur of early Cocteau Twins and the enveloping guitar treatments of Slowdive, Ferrucci finds sufficient room for her remarkably expressive voice.

There is tremendous emotional friction between the music’s gathering momentum and Ferrucci’s admission of romantic paralysis. Her delivery conveys the exhaustion of someone who has spent too much time negotiating with her own better judgment. As the instrumentation swells, the difficult business of accepting a lover’s indifference assumes almost orchestral proportions. Anyone who has ever mistaken emotional endurance for devotion should recognize the terrible predicament at its center.

Directed by Ferrucci herself, the accompanying video is a beautiful, surreal meditation in black and white, taking us to the seaside and through a series of enigmatic ceremonial gestures. The vastness of the coastal landscape lends a sense of solitude to the proceedings, while the dreamlike imagery gives physical expression to the emotional turmoil within the song. There is something quietly devastating about setting a song concerned with emotional paralysis against the perpetual movement of the sea, suggesting a world that continues along its course while we struggle to extricate ourselves from the past.

Watch the video for Motionless below:

Five of the album’s nine compositions originally appeared on the band’s self-produced, eponymous 2011 CDR. The remaining four, The Brightest Days, No Will, Bianca, and Embracing the Void, appeared in different arrangements on 2014’s Slanting Ray, released through Blood Rock Records and Manic Depression Records.

Fifteen years can radically alter one’s relationship with a song, particularly when the people responsible for its existence have accumulated an entirely new assortment of experiences. The enduring friendship between these four women gives their reunion considerable emotional significance, and their return to European stages offers younger listeners an opportunity to discover the band’s earlier incarnation in full flight.

The Brightest Days is out Saturday, November 28, on CD via Manic Depression Records, white vinyl via Icy Cold Records, and digitally. For Winter Severity Index, revisiting these compositions becomes an opportunity to discover how much life they still contain.

To celebrate this milestone, Winter Severity Index will be holding a release party in Rome at Traffic Club on 28 November.

items.fullText:
Imagine I was beautiful, compassion on display
Fashion for the cynical, passion how I weigh

Romance would be considerably easier to negotiate if everybody involved were issued a written itinerary, complete with scheduled moments of affection, designated hours for emotional catastrophes, and a little box to tick whenever somebody felt sufficiently attractive to be loved. Instead, we spend an obscene portion of our existence trying to decipher the intentions of people whose greatest accomplishment might be looking sensational in eyeliner. Fortunately, Astari Nite have a healthy appreciation for the absurdity of these transactions.

On Why Are You So Lame, from Medications In Bloom, Astari Nite indulge their fascination with the psychological misdemeanors of beautiful people, feeding romantic exasperation through the electrical apparatus of industrial rock and glam decadence.

Illia Tulloch’s arrangement possesses the nervous disposition of early Nine Inch Nails, back when Trent Reznor was still figuring out how much machinery he could cram into a pop song before somebody called an electrician. The guitars bristle with distortion, the rhythms twitch with impatience, and Mychael Ghost delivers his grievances with the delicious insolence of a disenchanted teenage idol. Somewhere between the pharmaceutical hysteria of Placebo, the theatrical liberties of David Bowie, and the bruised romanticism of The Smashing Pumpkins, Astari Nite finds ample room for their peculiar personality.

Ghost approaches beauty, rejection, magazine fantasies, and emotional negligence with an almost conversational irreverence. His affection for life’s ridiculous little complications gives the song its character, particularly when desire and disappointment become practically indistinguishable.

“The song is about my truth and friendship with people that I love,” says Mychael Ghost. “Time well spent with others. Engaging without fear.”

Such sentiments extend naturally from Astari Nite’s longstanding fascination with mental health, sexuality, love, and the occult. Their fondness for the alternative rock of the nineties also recalls an era when flamboyance and psychological disarray could coexist quite comfortably within the confines of a three-minute pop song.

The accompanying video embraces spontaneity, transforming a spell of backstage boredom into an impromptu excursion through the peculiar surroundings of a concert venue.

“The video…was captured rather quickly!” says Ghost. “Killing some time, about fourteen minutes’ worth, the band and I were able to film on my telephone. We had just finished sound-checking at a concert we were performing at and were greeted with maximum boredom moments after. So, we found ourselves wandering inside a unique, antique-like venue, roaming freely without a care in the world. What happened next was simply beautiful. I found myself in a land of make-believe, far away from home – lost, curious, and morbidly happy!”

Watch the video for Why Are You So Lame below:

Morbidly happy might be the perfect description of Astari Nite: a collection of incorrigible romantics making splendidly deranged music out of the inconvenience of having feelings.

Why Are You So Lame is the opening track on Medications In Bloom. Listen below and order it here.

Astari Nite will support Then Come Silence on a five-date U.K. run in May 2027.

  • May 26 — Newcastle, The Cluny
  • May 27 — Glasgow, Ivory Blacks
  • May 28 — Manchester, Club Academy
  • May 29 — London, The Garage (NFD’s 25th anniversary show)
  • May 30 — Bristol, Zed Alley

In the coming days, Ghost and Astari Nite bandmate Danny Ae will unveil We Are Every Color, a clothing line they conceived in response to the political and cultural divisions they saw around them in 2025.

“In the spring of 2025, Mychael Ghost and Danny Ae from Astari Nite faced an unfortunate cultural and human displacement governing the masses for what seems now a true eternity. A dividing, repressive, and inhuman force continued to take hold of our beloved human race, tribalizing every element of our world — from media to faith and, of course, politics.

Delivering a message through music has always been culturally daring, but even more so now as the message must fight the industry, the algorithm, censorship, and all the noise.

But what if we could share togetherness through fashion, friendship through design, strength through love, and embrace diversity? Unity in what makes us all oh so beautifully different.

If we could whisper to you once, intimately, that you are not alone, that we are all together — these fabrics with a sentiment would reveal that together… We are every color.”

items.title: Berlin-based Artist Boris Kaplunovich Asks Whose Lives We Hold Sacred in Video for “Let It Hurt”
items.summary: There´s no justice, no freedom At somebody else´s expense Washing off tears with tears, Blood with blood never made any sense There is an obscene convenience about the way human… The post Berlin-based Artist Boris Kaplunovich Asks Whose Lives We Hold Sacred in
items.fullText:
There´s no justice, no freedom
At somebody else´s expense
Washing off tears with tears,
Blood with blood never made any sense

There is an obscene convenience about the way human beings have learned to manufacture fresh grievances out of old wounds. Somebody gets killed, somebody builds a monument, somebody delivers a speech about the sanctity of human life, and before the flowers have wilted, somebody else is being fitted for a coffin. We’ve become frighteningly adept at compartmentalizing compassion, distributing it according to geographical boundaries and inherited allegiances. Even the dead are expected to carry passports.

Berlin-based singer-songwriter Boris Kaplunovich takes a considerable emotional inventory of this madness in Let It Hurt, the second single from his forthcoming debut EP, due in December. Born in Belarus and raised in Israel, Kaplunovich approaches the subject with the perspective of somebody for whom the notion of home has never been a particularly simple proposition. His experiences of geographical and emotional displacement inform a songwriting sensibility preoccupied with memory, belonging, and the increasingly difficult business of recognizing ourselves in other people.

Kaplunovich confronts the hypocrisy of protecting our own suffering while perpetuating the same horrors against others. Through images of wartime devastation, the lyrics examine collective denial, inherited hatred, and the futility of vengeance. Ultimately, he advocates dismantling tribal divisions, recognizing our shared humanity, and accepting pain as a means of fostering empathy, reconciliation, and healing rather than further bloodshed.

Working somewhere between the biblical bruising of Nick Cave and the Bad Seeds, the gothic intimacies of Chelsea Wolfe, and the exposed emotional nerve endings of Emma Ruth Rundle, Kaplunovich draws upon acoustic instrumentation, electronics, and the darker possibilities of post-punk. A multi-instrumentalist who builds his recordings from the ground up, he makes use of the tension between intimacy and enormity, between the private anguish of an individual and the collective sickness of a society that has institutionalized its suffering.

Let It Hurt suggests that pain might constitute a common language rather than another justification for segregation. It takes an odd kind of courage to advocate compassion when anger offers such immediate gratification. There’s a particularly devastating moral proposition at the song’s climax: vengeance cannot deliver justice, and purchasing your own peace with somebody else’s misery is a terrible bargain. The difficulty, of course, lies in accepting this when every institution around you seems determined to persuade you otherwise.

The accompanying video introduces a dark figure whose presence poses an uncomfortable question: are we witnessing somebody mourning the violent deaths of loved ones, or are we looking at hatred itself? Kaplunovich intends the figure to embody both, an unsettling acknowledgment of how readily legitimate grief can be recruited into the service of further atrocities.

Watch the video for Let It Hurt below:

Having shared stages with Micah P. Hinson and Matt Elliott, Kaplunovich belongs to a tradition of songwriters willing to investigate the less flattering aspects of our emotional lives. Here, he asks something considerably more demanding of us than sympathy for the afflicted: the recognition that somebody we have been instructed to despise might be suffering in precisely the same way we are. Imagine the trouble that simple admission could cause for the machinery of war.
